lead: A sinusoid is a voltage or current that rises and falls as a sine wave. Three numbers fix it: peak V<sub>m</sub> in volts, angular frequency ω in rad/s, and phase φ in degrees or radians. Its heating effect is not the peak. It is the RMS value, the steady DC that would heat a resistor equally. For a pure sine, RMS is peak divided by √2. Every AC meter, appliance rating and power calculation uses this value, so reading 230 V at a socket means an RMS value near 230 V and a peak near 325 V.
prereq: You need: the V-I relations of R, L and C (see circuit elements and their laws), and school trigonometry with the idea of an average taken by an integral.

blocks.text: Write a sinusoidal voltage as v(t) = V<sub>m</sub> sin(ωt + φ). V<sub>m</sub> is the peak value in volts, the largest value in either direction. ω is the angular frequency in rad/s. φ is the phase angle. Inside ωt + φ both terms must be in the same unit: with ω in rad/s, ωt is in radians, so turn φ into radians before adding (30° = π/6 = 0.524 rad). The same form works for current with I<sub>m</sub> and i(t).

v(t) is the instantaneous voltage in volts; V<sub>m</sub> is the peak voltage in volts; ω is the angular frequency in rad/s; t is time in seconds; φ is the phase angle; T is the period in seconds; f is the frequency in hertz.
Frequency f is in hertz, cycles per second. One cycle takes T = 1/f seconds. Angular frequency is ω = 2πf, so a 50 Hz supply has ω = 2π × 50 = 314 rad/s. A meter shows RMS, not peak.

Two sinusoids at the same frequency can be compared by phase. If v₁ reaches its peak before v₂, v₁ leads v₂. If it reaches later, v₁ lags v₂. The phase difference is measured in degrees or radians; 360° is one period.

Average value means the signed area under the curve over one interval divided by the interval length: area below the axis counts as negative. For a pure sine over a full period, the positive and negative halves cancel, so the full-cycle average is 0 V. Many exam questions mean the average over one half cycle, from 0 to T/2. That value is not zero.
V<sub>avg</sub> is the half-cycle average voltage in volts; V<sub>m</sub> is the peak voltage in volts; T is the period in seconds; ω is the angular frequency in rad/s.

RMS value is the square root of the mean of the square. Square the wave first, so sign disappears. Take the mean over one period, then the square root. This is the DC value that gives the same heating in a resistor. RMS is also called the effective value.
V<sub>rms</sub> is the RMS voltage in volts; v is the instantaneous voltage; T is the period in seconds; V<sub>m</sub> is the peak voltage in volts.

items: Square the sine: v² = Vm² sin²(ωt).
Use sin²θ = (1 − cos 2θ)/2. Over one period the cos 2θ term averages to zero.
The mean of the square is Vm²/2. Its square root is V<sub>m</sub>/√2.

blocks.text: Form factor compares RMS with average: form factor = V<sub>rms</sub> / V<sub>avg</sub>. For a pure sine it is 0.707/0.637 = 1.11. Some syllabi call it shape factor. Peak factor, also called crest factor, compares peak with RMS: peak factor = V<sub>m</sub> / V<sub>rms</sub>. For a sine it is 1.414.

A multimeter on AC range is calibrated to show RMS for a sine. On a distorted wave, a cheap meter may read the average and scale it by 1.11, so it lies. A true-RMS meter computes the heating value directly. Use RMS for power: P = Vrms² / R for a resistor, or P = Vrms Irms cos φ for a general AC load, where φ is now the angle between the voltage and the current, not the phase of v(t); power formulas come in 3.5.
Phasor diagrams use the same peak or RMS values consistently. Keep one choice. Most power work uses RMS; some textbooks draw phasors with peak. See 3.2 for phasors.

examples.question: An electric heater is connected to a supply v(t) = 325 sin(314t) V. Find the peak value, the RMS value, the average value over a half cycle, the form factor, the peak factor and the frequency.
steps: Compare v(t) with V<sub>m</sub> sin(ωt). The multiplier of the sine is V<sub>m</sub> = 325 V.
The coefficient of t is ω = 314 rad/s. Frequency f = ω/(2π) = 314/(2π) = 49.97 Hz ≈ 50 Hz.
RMS value V<sub>rms</sub> = V<sub>m</sub>/√2 = 325/1.414 = 229.8 V. This is the value an AC meter would show, close to the nominal 230 V.
examples.answer: V<sub>m</sub> = 325 V, V<sub>rms</sub> ≈ 229.8 V, V<sub>avg</sub>(half cycle) ≈ 206.9 V, form factor ≈ 1.11, peak factor ≈ 1.414, f ≈ 50 Hz.
examples.check:
import math
Vm = 325.0
omega = 314.0
f = omega/(2*math.pi)
Vrms = Vm/math.sqrt(2)
Vavg = 2*Vm/math.pi
ff = Vrms/Vavg
pf = Vm/Vrms
print(round(Vm, 0))
print(round(Vrms, 1))
print(round(f, 0))
print(round(Vavg, 1))
print(round(ff, 2))
print(round(pf, 3))

examples.question: A half-wave rectifier passes only the positive half cycles of v(t) = 325 sin(314t) V and gives 0 V for the negative half. Find the average value, the RMS value, the form factor and the peak factor of the output over one full period.
steps: One period is T = 2π/314 = 20 ms. The output is 325 sin(ωt) for 0 ≤ ωt ≤ π and 0 for π ≤ ωt ≤ 2π. Work in the angle θ = ωt, so one period is 2π.

Average: V<sub>avg</sub> = (1/2π) ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>π</sup> 325 sin θ dθ = (325/2π) [−cos θ]<sub>0</sub><sup>π</sup> = (325/2π) × 2 = 325/π = 103.5 V. The negative half adds zero area, so the average is half the half-cycle average of 206.9 V.
examples.answer: V<sub>avg</sub> = 103.5 V, V<sub>rms</sub> = 162.5 V, form factor = 1.57, peak factor = 2.00. These match the half-wave row of the table: 0.318 V<sub>m</sub> and 0.500 V<sub>m</sub>.

traps: Using the peak value where RMS belongs, such as in power, meter readings or impedance current.
Quoting zero as the average of a sine when the question means the half-cycle average; the full-cycle average of a pure sine is zero.
Mixing form factor and peak factor: form factor = RMS/average ≈ 1.11, peak factor = peak/RMS ≈ 1.414.
Forgetting that 230 V mains is RMS; the peak is about 325 V.
Applying sine factors to square, triangular or rectified waves; use their own table values.

quiz.q: Define peak value and RMS value of a sinusoid.
quiz.a: Peak value V<sub>m</sub> is the largest magnitude in either direction. RMS value is the square root of the mean of the square over one period; for a sine, V<sub>rms</sub> = V<sub>m</sub>/√2.

quiz.q: Why is the full-cycle average of a pure sine zero while the half-cycle average is 0.637Vm?
quiz.a: The positive and negative half cycles have equal area, so they cancel over a full period. Over one half cycle the area is positive and gives 2Vm/π = 0.637Vm.

quiz.q: A sine has V<sub>m</sub> = 100 V. Find V<sub>rms</sub>, the half-cycle average and the form factor.
quiz.a: V<sub>rms</sub> = 100/√2 = 70.7 V. Half-cycle average = 2 × 100/π = 63.7 V. Form factor = 70.7/63.7 = 1.11.

quiz.q: A 50 Hz sine has V<sub>rms</sub> = 120 V. Find ω and the peak value.
quiz.a: ω = 2πf = 2π × 50 = 314 rad/s. Peak V<sub>m</sub> = √2 × V<sub>rms</sub> = 1.414 × 120 = 169.7 V.

quiz.q: A cheap AC meter calibrated for a sine reads 100 V on a square wave of peak V<sub>m</sub>. It takes the half-cycle average and multiplies by 1.11. Find V<sub>m</sub> and the true RMS. Is the reading high or low?
quiz.a: Reading = 1.11Vm = 100 V, so V<sub>m</sub> = 90.1 V. True RMS of a square wave is V<sub>m</sub> = 90.1 V. The reading of 100 V is high by about 11%.

quiz.q: v₁ = 10 sin(314t) V and v₂ = 10 sin(314t − 45°) V. Which leads, and by how much?
quiz.a: v₁ leads v₂ by 45°. At a given time v₁ reaches its peak earlier than v₂ by 45° of the cycle.

quiz.q: Why do we use RMS rather than average for heating in a resistor?
quiz.a: Heating depends on current squared, so the sign of the current does not matter. RMS squares first, takes the mean and then the square root; it equals the DC value that gives the same heating.

quiz.q: State the form factor and peak factor of a pure sine.

beyond: Not for the exam. Digital energy meters sample the voltage and current waveform and compute RMS numerically, so they keep reading correctly when the wave is distorted. Power-quality instruments report crest factor and true RMS because switch-mode chargers and LED lamps draw non-sinusoidal current. Search for “true RMS measurement”, “crest factor” and “power quality harmonics” to go further. The same RMS idea extends to noise and vibration measurements in engineering.

figure.caption: The supply of the worked example over one 20 ms period. The RMS line (229.8 V) is the steady value that heats a resistor equally; the shorter line is the half-cycle average (206.9 V), whose rectangle has the same area as the shaded hump.

spec.aria: One cycle of 325 sin 314t from 0 to 20 ms with peak 325 V, a dashed RMS line at 229.8 V across the period and a half-cycle average line at 206.9 V over the first 10 ms.
